claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a single-phase simple solid solution with favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength of single-phase CoCrFeNiTi are primarily caused by a lack of significant dislocation obstacles.
Adding approximately 0.5 at% interstitial carbon to CoCrFeNiTi will increase lattice distortion.
Carbon-modified CoCrFeNiTi processed by MA and SPS will form fine nanoscale carbide precipitates.
The MA+SPS route will refine the grain microstructure of the alloy.
Interstitial-carbon-induced lattice distortion enhances solid-solution strengthening through stronger interactions with dislocations.
Nanoscale carbides provide nanoparticle or precipitation strengthening.
Carbon-induced lattice distortion and nanoscale carbides jointly impede dislocation motion during deformation.
Carbon may alter stacking-fault energy and favor TWIP or TRIP deformation mechanisms in CoCrFeNiTi.
Relative to identically processed carbon-free CoCrFeNiTi, the carbon-modified alloy will have higher hardness and yield strength.
The carbon-modified alloy will retain sufficient ductility for good plasticity despite its increased strength and hardness.
Microstructural characterization of the carbon-modified material should reveal refined grains and dispersed nanoscale carbides.
The proposed comparison applies to equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi processed by MA+SPS and tested under quasi-static room-temperature loading at comparable strain rates.
Carbon content must be limited to avoid formation of unintended brittle phases.
Carbon-free and approximately 0.5 at% carbon samples will be produced under identical MA+SPS conditions and compared by tensile testing, hardness testing, TEM, XRD, and EBSD.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase, or failure to observe the anticipated lattice distortion and nanoscale carbides, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
